title: Glutathione for Hangover: Does It Work? Absorption, Liposomal, NAC
excerpt: Alcohol really does drain glutathione, but does a glutathione supplement help a hangover? What the research says about absorption, liposomal and IV forms, and NAC as a cheaper precursor.
metaDescription: Does glutathione help a hangover? Why alcohol drains it, why oral glutathione absorbs poorly, what liposomal and IV claims miss, and where NAC fits.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** glutathione really is one of the main tools your liver uses to cope with alcohol, and heavy drinking really does drain it. But that doesn't mean swallowing a glutathione pill will help your hangover. Ordinary oral glutathione is poorly absorbed, the studies that show it raising body levels took weeks or months of daily use, and there are no good human trials testing glutathione (oral, liposomal, or IV) as a hangover remedy. If you want to support glutathione, the better-studied route is giving your body the building blocks to make its own, mainly through cysteine sources like NAC. Even that has only thin hangover evidence. This guide walks through what's real, what's marketing, and what to do instead.

**The quick version of what to do:** Don't expect a glutathione capsule taken the night you drink to change how you feel the next morning. If you want to try something in this space, NAC (N-acetylcysteine) or L-cysteine has slightly more relevant evidence and costs less, though the hangover data is still small. Skip "hangover IV" glutathione pushes, which add cost and needle risk without trial evidence. The things that reliably reduce hangovers are still drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and sleeping.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before taking glutathione or NAC if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have asthma, have liver or kidney disease, take nitroglycerin or blood thinners, are on chemotherapy, or drink heavily on most days. If you drink heavily on a regular basis, a supplement is not a substitute for medical care, and stopping suddenly can be dangerous, so get help from a clinician. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Glutathione Is and Why It Matters When You Drink

Glutathione is a small molecule your body makes from three amino acids: glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. Almost every cell makes it, and the liver makes and stores a lot of it. It's often called the body's "master antioxidant," which is marketing language, but there's real substance behind it. Glutathione does two jobs that matter for drinking:

1. **It neutralizes reactive molecules.** When cells are under oxidative stress (a build-up of unstable, damaging molecules often called free radicals), glutathione donates electrons to calm them down.
2. **It helps the liver detoxify.** Liver enzymes attach glutathione to harmful compounds so they can be made safe and flushed out. This is the same system that cleans up the toxic by-product of acetaminophen (Tylenol), which is why glutathione comes up so often in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

Of the three building blocks, **cysteine is usually the limiting one.** Your body tends to have plenty of glutamate and glycine, so how much glutathione you can make depends heavily on how much cysteine is available. Keep that in mind, because it's the whole reason NAC exists as an alternative.

## Does Alcohol Really Deplete Glutathione?

Yes, this part of the story is well supported. Here's how alcohol leans on your glutathione supply.

### Acetaldehyde and oxidative stress

Your liver breaks alcohol down in two steps. First, alcohol becomes **acetaldehyde**, a toxic and reactive compound. Then acetaldehyde is converted to acetate, which is relatively harmless. Acetaldehyde is one of the suspected contributors to hangover symptoms like nausea, flushing, and a pounding heart, though researchers still debate how big its role is in an ordinary hangover.

Acetaldehyde can bind to glutathione and to cysteine, and the process of breaking down alcohol also produces extra oxidative stress in liver cells. Both of these use up glutathione. One of the alcohol-processing enzymes, **CYP2E1**, becomes more active in people who drink heavily on a regular basis, and it's a well-known source of these reactive molecules.

### Heavy, long-term drinking is where depletion is clearest

Most of the strong evidence for glutathione depletion comes from **chronic heavy drinking**: animal studies, liver biopsies, and studies of people with alcohol-related liver disease. Research groups studying alcoholic liver injury have shown for decades that long-term alcohol exposure lowers glutathione, especially inside the mitochondria (the energy-producing parts of liver cells), and that this makes cells more vulnerable to damage. Poor nutrition, which often goes along with heavy drinking, makes it worse because it means less cysteine coming in.

### What about one night out?

This is where the hangover marketing gets ahead of the science. A single evening of drinking does put some extra demand on glutathione, and fasting makes the dip larger. But there's no good human evidence showing that the glutathione drop from one night of social drinking is a main *cause* of your hangover, or that topping it up fixes the hangover. Hangovers involve several things at once: dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, acetaldehyde, and the after-effects of alcohol on brain chemistry. Glutathione is one thread in that knot, not the whole thing.

So the first half of the supplement pitch ("alcohol uses up glutathione") is true. The second half ("so take glutathione to prevent a hangover") doesn't follow automatically. It depends on whether a supplement actually raises glutathione where it matters, quickly enough to make a difference. That's the next problem.

## The Big Problem: Oral Glutathione Absorption

Glutathione is a peptide, which means it's a short chain of amino acids. Your digestive system is built to break peptides apart. Enzymes in the gut lining, particularly one called gamma-glutamyl transferase, chop glutathione back into its individual amino acids before much of it can reach your bloodstream intact.

### The early study that started the doubt

A frequently cited study by Witschi and colleagues, published in the *European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology* in 1992, gave healthy volunteers a single large oral dose of glutathione (3 grams) and measured blood levels afterward. Blood glutathione didn't meaningfully rise. The authors concluded that, in humans, a single oral dose wasn't an effective way to raise circulating glutathione.

A later randomized trial by Allen and Bradley in the *Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine* (2011) gave adults 500 mg of oral glutathione twice a day for four weeks. They found no significant change in markers of oxidative stress, including blood glutathione levels, compared with placebo.

### The study that pushed back

The picture isn't completely negative. A six-month randomized trial by Richie and colleagues, published in the *European Journal of Nutrition* in 2015, gave adults 250 mg or 1,000 mg of oral glutathione daily. Over months, glutathione stores in blood, red blood cells, and cheek cells went up, more so at the higher dose, and levels fell back toward baseline after people stopped.

How do these fit together? One reasonable reading is that some glutathione (or its breakdown products) does get used, and that steady daily intake can slowly raise body stores over weeks to months. What the studies don't show is a quick spike after a single dose.

### Why this matters for a hangover

A hangover is a one-night problem. The only trials suggesting oral glutathione raises body stores needed **months of daily use**, and none of them measured hangovers. Taking a glutathione capsule before bed after a night out is not what those studies tested, and the single-dose study suggests it wouldn't do much to your blood levels in that time frame.

## Liposomal Glutathione: Does It Fix the Absorption Problem?

"Liposomal" glutathione is the industry's answer to the absorption complaint. A liposome is a tiny bubble made of fat-like molecules (similar to the material in cell membranes). The idea is that wrapping glutathione in these bubbles protects it from being broken down in the gut and helps it get absorbed.

### What the evidence shows

The best-known human study is a small pilot by Sinha and colleagues, published in the *European Journal of Clinical Nutrition* in 2018. Healthy adults took liposomal glutathione daily for a month. Glutathione levels in blood and some cells rose, and some markers of oxidative stress and immune function moved in a favorable direction. It's an encouraging early result, and it supports the idea that liposomal forms can raise body stores.

The limits are important, though:

- **It was small and short, without a proper placebo group.** Pilot studies are meant to justify bigger trials, not settle questions.
- **It measured body stores over weeks, not hangover symptoms.** Nobody has shown that liposomal glutathione taken around a night of drinking makes you feel better the next day.
- **Quality varies a lot between products.** "Liposomal" isn't a regulated standard. Some products contain well-formed liposomes, and some are mostly marketing. You usually can't tell from the label.
- **It's expensive.** Liposomal glutathione often costs several times more per dose than plain glutathione or NAC.

### Our honest take on liposomal claims

Claims that liposomal glutathione "absorbs 10x better" or "works within minutes" for a hangover are not backed by hangover research. The fair statement is: liposomal forms *may* raise body glutathione better than plain capsules over weeks of daily use, based on limited data. That's a reasonable thing to say on a general wellness product. It is not evidence that it prevents or treats hangovers.

## What About Sublingual, Spray, and IV Glutathione?

### Sublingual and spray forms

Some products are meant to dissolve under the tongue or be sprayed in the mouth, on the idea that they skip the gut. There's very little published human research on these forms, and nothing on hangovers. Treat claims about them as unproven.

### Glutathione IV drips and "hangover IV" clinics

IV glutathione bypasses the gut completely, so absorption isn't the issue. Many hangover IV services add a glutathione "push" for an extra charge. A few points worth knowing before you pay for one:

- **There are no good controlled trials of IV glutathione for hangovers.** Most of the relief people feel from a hangover IV likely comes from the fluids, and sometimes from anti-nausea or pain medication added to the bag. Drinking water and an electrolyte drink gets you a lot of the fluid benefit for far less money.
- **IV glutathione is short-lived in the blood.** Studies of IV glutathione show it's cleared from the bloodstream fairly quickly, so a one-off push isn't a lasting "reload."
- **Any IV has real risks.** Infection, vein irritation, bruising, and rare allergic reactions are possible. The FDA has also warned about quality problems with some compounded glutathione products in the past. If you choose an IV, use a licensed medical provider, not a pop-up.
- **It's not a safe workaround for heavy drinking.** If you find yourself needing IVs to function after drinking, that's a signal to talk to a doctor about your drinking, not a supplement problem.

## NAC: The Precursor Alternative

Since cysteine is the limiting building block, one way to support glutathione is to supply cysteine rather than glutathione itself. That's what **N-acetylcysteine (NAC)** does. It's a stable form of cysteine that's well absorbed and that the body uses to make its own glutathione.

### Why NAC has a stronger foundation than oral glutathione

- **It's a real medicine.** IV and oral NAC is the standard hospital antidote for acetaminophen overdose. It works by refilling the liver's glutathione supply. That use is done in a hospital, under medical supervision, at doses far higher than any supplement, and a daily NAC capsule is not a substitute for emergency treatment.
- **It reliably raises glutathione when the body is low.** Because the body controls how much glutathione it makes, NAC tends to help most when stores are depleted, which is the situation alcohol creates.
- **It's cheap.** NAC is usually a fraction of the cost of liposomal glutathione.

### What the hangover evidence actually says

The evidence for NAC specifically for hangovers is small:

- A randomized, placebo-controlled trial by Coppersmith and colleagues, published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2021, tested NAC taken around drinking. The results suggested some benefit, but the trial was small and the effect wasn't consistent across everyone studied. It's a reason to study NAC further, not proof that it works.
- A related amino acid, **L-cysteine**, was tested in a small randomized trial by Eriksson and colleagues, also in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* (2020). It reported improvements in some hangover symptoms, including headache and anxiety. Again, the trial was small.
- A 2022 systematic review of hangover treatments in the journal *Addiction* (Roberts and colleagues) looked across the published trials and rated the evidence for every remedy it found, L-cysteine included, as very low quality. No hangover remedy, glutathione-related or otherwise, came out with strong evidence.

So NAC and L-cysteine have *a little* hangover-specific research, which is more than oral glutathione has. That's a modest edge, not a strong recommendation. We compare NAC and DHM in more depth in our [NAC vs DHM guide](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025).

### NAC safety and regulatory status

- **Common side effects** are stomach upset, nausea, and occasionally diarrhea. NAC also has a strong sulfur smell some people dislike.
- **Asthma:** inhaled NAC can trigger airway spasms. Oral NAC is less of a concern, but people with asthma should check with a doctor.
- **Medication interactions:** NAC may increase the headache and blood-pressure-lowering effects of nitroglycerin, and there's a theoretical concern about bleeding risk with blood thinners. Ask your pharmacist if you take either.
- **Supplement status:** in the US, NAC was approved as a drug before it was sold as a supplement, which led the FDA to question whether it could legally be sold as one. In 2022 the agency said it would not take enforcement action against NAC supplements, so it remains widely available over the counter, though that status has been debated.

### Timing, if you try it

The small trials gave NAC or L-cysteine around the time of drinking rather than the next morning, on the logic that the body needs the building block while it's processing alcohol. Follow the product label for dose. If you take any medications or have a health condition, check with a pharmacist first.

## Glutathione vs NAC vs DHM: How They Compare

These three often get lumped together, but they work in different ways and have different evidence behind them.

| | Oral glutathione | NAC | DHM |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | The antioxidant itself | A cysteine source for making glutathione | A plant compound from Japanese raisin tree |
| **Absorption** | Poor as a single dose; may raise stores with months of daily use | Well absorbed | Fairly low, though studied orally |
| **Hangover-specific human trials** | None we know of | Small trials (NAC and L-cysteine) with mixed results | Limited; most evidence is from animal and lab studies |
| **Other human evidence** | Small trials on body stores and fatty liver | Long medical use as an acetaminophen antidote | A 2015 trial in people with fatty liver found some marker improvements |
| **Typical cost** | Moderate to high (liposomal is highest) | Low | Low to moderate |

DHM (dihydromyricetin) works through a different mechanism than glutathione. Animal research suggests it may affect how the brain responds to alcohol and may support the liver enzymes that clear alcohol and acetaldehyde. Most of that evidence comes from rodent and lab studies, and the human data is limited, so we describe it as promising rather than proven. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when.

Some products combine approaches. For example, [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) pairs DHM with L-cysteine, the same glutathione building block tested in the small L-cysteine trial mentioned above. If you'd rather keep it simple and cheaper, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is DHM on its own. Neither is a substitute for drinking less, and neither will prevent a hangover after heavy drinking.

## Should You Take Glutathione Before or After Drinking?

If you've decided to try oral glutathione anyway, here's the honest answer on timing: **there's no hangover evidence for any timing.** A few reasonable points:

- **One dose around a night out is unlikely to matter much.** The only studies showing oral glutathione raising body levels used daily doses for weeks or months.
- **If you're interested in glutathione for general liver support,** it's a daily, long-term supplement, not a hangover pill. Our guide to the [best liver supplements](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) puts the options in context.
- **Food matters more than the capsule.** Eating protein before drinking slows alcohol absorption and supplies amino acids, including cysteine. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the evidence.

For a broader look at what's worth taking ahead of a night out, see our guide to [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking).

## Can Glutathione Protect Your Liver From Alcohol?

This is a separate question from hangovers, and the answer is still "not proven."

- **Fatty liver research.** A small open-label pilot study by Honda and colleagues in *BMC Gastroenterology* (2017) gave oral glutathione to people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease for four months and saw improvements in a liver enzyme (ALT) in some participants. It had no placebo group, and it wasn't about alcohol.
- **Alcohol-related liver disease.** NAC has been studied in hospital settings for severe alcoholic hepatitis, alongside standard treatment, with mixed results. That's serious illness managed by specialists, and it says nothing about whether a supplement protects a social drinker's liver.

There's no supplement that makes regular heavy drinking safe for your liver. If you drink heavily, the step that protects your liver is drinking less, and a doctor can check your liver with a simple blood test.

## Who Should Be Careful With Glutathione and NAC

Glutathione and NAC are generally well tolerated at label doses, but check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you:

- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** There isn't enough safety research on supplemental glutathione in pregnancy.
- **Have asthma.** Inhaled glutathione and inhaled NAC have been linked to airway tightening. Ask before using oral forms too.
- **Take nitroglycerin or blood thinners.** NAC may interact with both.
- **Are being treated for cancer.** Antioxidant supplements may interact with some chemotherapy and radiation treatments, so don't add them without your oncologist's okay.
- **Have liver or kidney disease.** Your care team should decide what's appropriate.
- **Drink heavily most days.** Supplements can't offset the harm of heavy drinking, and alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous. A clinician can help you cut back safely.

Glutathione is also sold for skin lightening, sometimes as injections. That use isn't related to hangovers and has its own safety concerns. Don't get glutathione injections from unlicensed providers.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover

If you came here looking for a fix, here's where the evidence is strongest, roughly in order:

1. **Drink less, and drink slower.** The total amount of alcohol and how fast you drink it are the biggest factors in how bad a hangover gets.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption.
3. **Alternate with water.** It won't prevent a hangover on its own, but dehydration makes symptoms worse.
4. **Choose clearer drinks.** Darker drinks tend to carry more by-products of fermentation that may worsen hangovers.
5. **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, and poor sleep is a big part of how bad the next day feels.
6. **Be careful with painkillers.** If you need one the next morning, follow the label, and read our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before reaching for acetaminophen.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes into each of these, and our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025) rates the evidence for the most popular products.

## The Bottom Line

Glutathione is genuinely important to how your liver handles alcohol, and heavy drinking genuinely drains it. But oral glutathione is poorly absorbed in a single dose, the trials showing it raises body stores needed months of daily use, liposomal versions have only small pilot data, and nothing in this category has been shown in good human trials to prevent or treat a hangover. If you want to support glutathione, NAC or L-cysteine is the cheaper, better-studied route, with a small amount of hangover research behind it. For actual hangover prevention, the basics still do most of the work. And if you're drinking enough that you're looking for liver protection, that's worth a conversation with your doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does glutathione help with hangovers?**

There are no good human trials showing that glutathione supplements prevent or treat hangovers. Alcohol does use up glutathione, especially with heavy, long-term drinking, but oral glutathione is poorly absorbed as a single dose. The studies showing it raises body levels used daily doses for weeks or months and didn't measure hangovers.

**Is liposomal glutathione better for a hangover?**

Liposomal glutathione may raise body glutathione better than plain capsules, based on a small one-month pilot study published in 2018. But that study measured body stores, not hangover symptoms, and product quality varies widely. There's no evidence that liposomal glutathione taken around a night of drinking prevents a hangover.

**Is NAC better than glutathione for a hangover?**

NAC is better absorbed, cheaper, and has a little hangover-specific research, including a small 2021 randomized trial with mixed results. That's more than oral glutathione has, but it's still weak evidence. NAC can cause stomach upset and may interact with nitroglycerin and blood thinners, so check with a pharmacist first if you take medications.

**Should I take glutathione before or after drinking?**

There's no hangover research supporting any timing. A single dose around a night out is unlikely to make much difference, because the studies showing oral glutathione raising body levels used daily doses over weeks or months. Eating a meal with protein before drinking is a better-supported step.

**Does a glutathione IV help a hangover?**

There are no good controlled trials of IV glutathione for hangovers. Most of the relief from a hangover IV likely comes from the fluids and any anti-nausea or pain medicine added. IV glutathione is also cleared from the blood fairly quickly. Any IV carries risks like infection and bruising, so only use a licensed medical provider.

**Does alcohol deplete glutathione?**

Yes. Breaking down alcohol produces acetaldehyde and extra oxidative stress, both of which use up glutathione. The depletion is clearest in people who drink heavily over long periods, and poor nutrition makes it worse. A single night of social drinking causes a smaller, temporary dip.

**Can glutathione protect my liver if I drink regularly?**

It hasn't been shown to. A small pilot study found oral glutathione improved a liver enzyme in some people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, but that wasn't about alcohol and had no placebo group. No supplement makes regular heavy drinking safe for your liver. Drinking less is what protects it, and a doctor can check your liver with a blood test.

**Is glutathione safe to take with alcohol?**

At label doses, oral glutathione is generally well tolerated, and there's no known dangerous interaction with alcohol itself. Check with a doctor first if you're pregnant, have asthma, are being treated for cancer, or have liver or kidney disease. Taking it doesn't make heavy drinking any safer.
